body.value:
This page explains how to become a carer in Ireland.

It covers both family (unpaid) carers and professional (paid) carers, and outlines the supports, training and steps involved.
Decide what type of carer you want to be

There are two main types of carers in Ireland:

  • family or unpaid carers – people who provide full-time care to a relative, partner, friend or neighbour who needs support due to age, illness or disability
  • professional or paid carers – people who work as carers or healthcare assistants in homes, community services, nursing homes or healthcare settings

The steps and requirements differ depending on which path you choose.
Understand the role of a carer

A carer provides support to someone who needs help because of age, illness, or disability. This can include:

  • personal care (washing, dressing and eating)
  • helping with mobility and daily routines
  • emotional support and companionship
  • supporting independence and wellbeing

Family carers do not need formal qualifications. Professional carers usually require recognised training.
Check eligibility for carer payments and supports (family carers)

If you provide full-time care, you may qualify for financial supports from the Department of Social Protection.

Carer's Allowance

A weekly, means-tested payment for people on low income who provide full-time care and attention.

You must:

  • be 18 or over
  • provide full-time care and attention (at least ~35 hours per week)
  • meet residency and means test conditions

More information: Carer's Allowance

Carer's Benefit

A payment for people who leave work or reduce hours to care for someone full-time. This is not means-tested but requires sufficient PRSI contributions.

More information: Carer's Benefit

Carer's Support Grant

An annual lump sum payment for full-time carers who meet certain qualifying conditions.

More information: Carer's Support Grant

If you want to work professionally as a carer, most employers and public services expect you to have a QQI-accredited qualification.

Recommended qualification

The qualification you should get is a QQI Level 5 Certificate in Healthcare Support (Major Award).

This qualification is awarded by Quality and Qualifications Ireland. It is the standard qualification for many professional carer roles, including Health Care Assistant jobs throughout Ireland.

The QQI Level 5 award includes training in:

  • care skills and personal support
  • health and safety
  • communication
  • work experience

Many employers – including the Health Service Executive (HSE) – list this qualification as essential or highly desirable.

You can take this course at further education colleges or approved training providers across Ireland.

Get more information on the HSE healthcare assistant pathway.

Professional carer roles typically require:

  • Garda Vetting / Garda clearance (essential for working with vulnerable adults)
  • proof of the right to work in Ireland (legal work status)
  • good spoken and written English

These checks help protect people receiving care and are standard for professional carer jobs.
Apply for carer or healthcare assistant roles

Once you have the appropriate training and checks, you can apply for roles such as:

  • Health Care Assistant (HCA)
  • Home Support Worker
  • Community Carer
  • Residential Care Worker

Jobs are available through:

  • the HSE and HSE-funded services
  • nursing homes and residential care settings
  • home-care providers

Public-sector and funded roles are advertised through official HSE recruitment channels.
Continue learning and developing your skills

Many carers continue to develop their skills through:

  • additional training (for example: in dementia care, palliative care, or disability care)
  • on-the-job training provided by employers
  • courses in manual handling and infection prevention

Ongoing learning improves career progression and quality of care.
